title: GPan-LoRA: Gaussian Process Amortized Networks for Bayesian Low-Rank Adaptation in Large Language Models
one_liner: Fine-tune a large language model with low-rank adapters while keeping uncertainty estimates calibrated on unfamiliar inputs.
lead: Low-rank adaptation changes only a small set of weights inside a large language model, which keeps fine-tuning cheap. The missing piece is uncertainty: after fine-tuning, the model should say when it is unsure instead of giving a confident wrong answer on inputs that differ from its training data. This paper builds a Bayesian version of LoRA that keeps track of uncertainty at the function level, not only at the weight level. It does that with a Gaussian process (a Bayesian function model that assigns both a prediction and an uncertainty level to each input) and an amortized network (a helper network that predicts variational parameters, meaning the numbers used to approximate a hard Bayesian update).

paras: Ordinary LoRA fine-tuning gives you a single updated model. That is enough if you only want the most likely answer. It is not enough if you need to know how much trust to place in that answer, because one set of adapter weights cannot express the range of functions still plausible after seeing limited training data.

Earlier Bayesian LoRA methods ran into two opposite problems. Some approximated the full Bayesian update with local curvature around one solution, which scales poorly and can miss far-away uncertainty. Others used cheaper approximations that run at scale but distort the posterior (posterior means the updated uncertainty after seeing data), so the model stays too confident when the test inputs differ from the training inputs because the approximation removes uncertainty that should remain on poorly supported functions.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Represent the LoRA update as a Gaussian process over functions and use an amortized variational network so the Bayesian update stays scalable while preserving uncertainty semantics.

panels.title: 1. Start from frozen base model
panels.viz_args: Large language model stays fixed; only small low-rank adapters are trainable.
panels.caption: The method keeps the usual LoRA computational budget.

panels.title: 2. Need uncertainty, not only a point estimate
panels.caption: A plain adapter can answer confidently even when the new input pattern is outside what it learned.

panels.title: 3. Put a Gaussian process over the adapter function
panels.viz_args: Each adapter input gets a predictive mean and predictive variance from a Bayesian function model.
panels.caption: Uncertainty is attached to the function the adapter computes, not only to one weight setting.

panels.title: 4. Use an amortized network to predict the variational terms
panels.caption: The helper network shares computation across examples, so the Bayesian approximation can scale.

panels.title: 5. Get calibrated uncertainty after fine-tuning
panels.caption: The model keeps task accuracy while becoming less overconfident on shifted data.

steps.b: Freeze the base model and insert LoRA adapters
steps.text: Only the low-rank update path is trainable, so the method starts from the same economical setup used in standard LoRA.

steps.b: Model the adapter output with a Gaussian process
steps.text: For each adapter input, maintain a predictive mean and predictive uncertainty instead of a single deterministic output.
Use a small learned set of inducing points, meaning representative inputs that summarize the Gaussian process, because the full Bayesian update over all training inputs is too costly.

steps.b: Predict approximation terms with an amortized network
steps.text: A helper network maps each example to the parameters of the variational approximation, so the method avoids solving a separate optimization problem for every input.

Update the adapter, inducing points, and helper network together so the model fits the task data while keeping uncertainty tied to the Gaussian-process prior, meaning the uncertainty pattern assumed before seeing task data, because the objective rewards label fit but also penalizes unjustified departure from that prior.

paras: The paper changes what a LoRA adapter represents. Instead of learning only one low-rank weight update, it learns a probability distribution over adapter functions, which means the fine-tuned model can return both a prediction and a calibrated uncertainty estimate.
object.object: LoRA adaptation from a single function to a Bayesian family of functions

hidden.name: how much uncertainty should remain after fine-tuning
paras: The central quantity is not raw task loss. It is how much uncertainty the model should still carry after seeing the fine-tuning data. If the method collapses uncertainty too aggressively, it will act certain on unfamiliar inputs. If it keeps too much uncertainty everywhere, it will become hesitant even where the data is clear.

GPan-LoRA tries to place that uncertainty in the right parts of the input space. Inputs close to well-supported training cases should have low predictive variance, which means low spread in plausible outputs. Inputs far from those cases should keep higher predictive variance because the Bayesian function model has less evidence there.

heat.caption: Dark cells show places where the method should keep or reduce uncertainty according to how much evidence the fine-tuning data provides.

reads.html: The method should stay confident where the fine-tuning data really supports a decision and stay cautious where the input looks unfamiliar.

The Gaussian-process posterior allocates predictive variance according to evidence from the inducing-point summary and the learned variational update, because those terms decide how strongly the data overrides the prior.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: uncertainty is attached to functions, not only weights
paras: A weight-space approximation often becomes overconfident because many different weight settings can produce similar outputs near the training data while behaving very differently away from it. If the approximation focuses on one local region of weight space, it can underestimate how many plausible functions remain.

The Gaussian-process view avoids that collapse by modeling the adapter as a function directly. For any new input, the prediction is built from its relation to the inducing points. If the new input resembles regions supported by the training data, the function value is strongly constrained and uncertainty drops. If the input is far from that support, the prior still matters and uncertainty stays higher.

The amortized network matters because variational inference (inference means computing or approximating the Bayesian update) would otherwise require too much work per example. By learning a shared mapping from example features to variational parameters, the model can approximate the update in one forward pass, so the scalable computation and the Bayesian semantics remain coupled.

stages.s: Task examples enter the frozen base model and LoRA adapter
Adapter outputs are treated as a Gaussian-process function
Inducing points summarize the training evidence
Amortized network predicts the variational update terms
Posterior predictive mean and variance are computed for each new input
Fine-tuned predictions with uncertainty that tracks evidence density

math.words: The method maximizes a variational objective: fit the labeled task data well while keeping the approximate Bayesian update close to the Gaussian-process prior.
math.equation: ELBO = E_q(f)[log p(y | x, f)] - KL(q(u) || p(u))
symbols: the approximate posterior over adapter functions after seeing task data
the likelihood of the labels under function f
the inducing-point values that summarize the Gaussian process
the learned approximate posterior over those inducing values
the prior distribution over inducing values before task data
a divergence that measures how far the approximation moves from the prior

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one batch contains examples the model has seen many times. The data-fit term rises when the adapter predicts their labels well.
If the approximation also moves far away from the prior at every inducing point, the KL term rises and the objective falls.
Training seeks a balance: explain the labels, but only use as much posterior change as the evidence justifies.
That balance matters because it keeps uncertainty from collapsing in weakly supported regions.

math.note: The first term rewards task fit. The second term limits unjustified certainty because the approximate posterior must still resemble the prior unless the data clearly supports a change.

charts.title: Plain or weakly Bayesian LoRA
charts.note: Earlier methods can fit the training task while staying too certain on inputs that differ from the fine-tuning set.

charts.title: GPan-LoRA
charts.note: The gain comes from keeping function-level uncertainty aligned with evidence density, so the model lowers confidence where the training signal is weak because sparse evidence cannot justify a sharp posterior there.

items.b: Inducing points may miss important regions.
items.html: If the sparse support set does not cover the task inputs well, the Gaussian process will place uncertainty in the wrong places because its summary of the training evidence is incomplete.

items.b: The amortized network can underfit the variational update.
items.html: A weak helper network may predict poor variational parameters, which means the scalable approximation no longer matches the intended Bayesian update.

items.b: Calibration can still break under very large shift.
items.html: If the test inputs are far outside both the pretraining and fine-tuning regimes, the prior assumptions of the adapter function may no longer reflect the true uncertainty pattern.

Choose inducing points that cover the task inputs, train the helper network until the variational approximation is stable, and evaluate calibration on shifted data because the method is meant to control confidence, not only accuracy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a small language classification task and fine-tune the same base model in three ways: plain LoRA, a simple Bayesian LoRA baseline, and GPan-LoRA. Create one test split close to the fine-tuning data and a second split with altered wording, topic mix, or label balance.

Log both accuracy and confidence calibration on both splits. The demo should show that GPan-LoRA stays competitive on the familiar split and reduces overconfident mistakes on the shifted split because its uncertainty remains tied to how much direct evidence the function model has seen.
demo.metric_eq: ece_gap = ECE_shifted - ECE_familiar ; overconfident_error_rate = confident_wrong / total_predictions
demo.closing: The key evidence is not only higher accuracy. It is lower confidence on weakly supported cases and fewer confident wrong answers after the input pattern changes, because calibrated uncertainty should react when the model sees inputs far from the fine-tuning evidence.
